newsitem.title: USA: USDA data left US soyoil exports overpriced -trade.
newsitem.headline: USDA data left US soyoil exports overpriced -trade.

text.p: Forecasts from the U.S. Department of Agriculture that showed a drop in U.S. soybean ending stocks have left U.S. soyoil too expensive for most foreign buyers, U.S. exporters said.
"It (U.S. export business) doesn't make economic sense for anybody right now," said one U.S. export source.

On January 10, USDA reported 1996/97 soybean ending stocks were 155 million bushels. That figure was the lowest since 1976/77 and drove soyoil futures on the Chicago Board of Trade up the daily 1.00 cent per lb limit the day of the report.
Although the soyoil market has lost some of its loft, prices have still not fallen to the levels that were traded before the USDA report.

One exporter estimated that at current prices, U.S. soyoil is $25.00 per tonne more expensive than South America supplies, so the CBOT market would have to fall 1.00 to 1.25 cents a pound before the U.S. could become competitive again.
Exporters said that China has been an active buyer in South American markets, but has not purchased significant quantities of U.S. soyoil since December because of high costs and current supplies.
Supplies of soyoil and soymeal in China are currently seen as adequate, so that nation was not expected to re-enter U.S. markets in the near term.
"I really don't see China back in the oil market until after the Chinese New Year," the exporter said.
The Chinese New Year ends in mid-February, sources said.
